opus-5.5.text:
I think architecture is actually the deciding factor, more than the idea of MTP itself. Multi-token prediction as a concept has been around for a while — the intuition is very natural: if the model only learns to predict the next token, it can be a bit short-sighted, so asking it to look a few tokens ahead gives it a denser training signal and pushes it to plan a little. But whether it becomes mainstream depends on whether you can fit it into the architecture cheaply and make it pay off in more than one place.

Early versions used parallel independent heads on top of the shared trunk, and the problem was that those heads don't really talk to each other — the prediction of token t+2 doesn't condition on what you predicted for t+1. So the gains were inconsistent, especially at smaller scales, and people treated it as a research curiosity. What changed things, in my view, is designing the MTP modules sequentially, so each extra depth keeps the causal chain — it takes the previous representation plus the embedding of the next token and predicts one step further. That keeps the training objective coherent with how the model actually generates text.

The second part is the cost. If MTP adds a lot of parameters or slows training, nobody will adopt it. But if the modules are lightweight, share the embedding and output head with the main model, and you can simply drop them at inference time, then the downside is small. And then there's an upside on the inference side: those same modules can serve as a draft model for speculative decoding. If the acceptance rate is high, you get a real speedup basically for free. That dual role — better training signal plus faster decoding — is what makes it attractive to production teams, not just researchers.

So I'd say MTP becomes mainstream not because everyone suddenly believes in "predicting the future," but because the architecture makes it cheap, compatible with things like MoE and efficient attention, and useful at deployment. Once a few strong open models show that it works at scale and the engineering is clean, others follow. The remaining questions are more about how many tokens ahead is worth it, and how it interacts with things like RL fine-tuning and long reasoning — those are still open, and I think the answers will again come from architecture choices rather than from the objective alone.

r001.rationale: The response says MTP’s architecture should account for deployment needs: lightweight modules that can be dropped at inference or used for speculative decoding make the design attractive. It presents those requirements as guiding whether the architecture is adopted for training.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that MTP, multi-token prediction, is not really an architecture question on its own. It's a question of whether the architecture around it is willing to pay for it, and whether the training objective and the inference system agree on what it's for.

When we did it in DeepSeek-V3, the design choice that mattered most was keeping the MTP modules causal and sharing the embedding and output head with the main model. That sounds like a small engineering detail, but it changes the economics completely. If each extra prediction head is a full, independent branch, you're adding parameters and FLOPs that only help you at training time, and most teams will cut it the moment they're under compute pressure. If instead the extra module is lightweight, sits on top of the main trunk, and reuses the representations the model is already computing, then the marginal cost is small and the benefit shows up in two places at once: a denser training signal, and a speculative decoding draft you get almost for free.

So I'd frame it this way. MTP becomes mainstream when the architecture treats it as part of the main model rather than as an auxiliary trick. Three things push in that direction.

First, MoE. Sparse models have a very particular problem: the active parameter count is small, so the per-token compute is cheap, but memory bandwidth at inference is still dominated by loading experts. Anything that lets you emit more tokens per forward pass is disproportionately valuable there. MTP as a draft mechanism fits MoE much better than it fits a dense model of the same quality, so as more of the frontier moves to sparse architectures, the incentive to keep MTP grows.

Second, the attention and KV-cache design. Something like MLA, where the cache is compressed, reduces the cost of verifying several draft tokens at once. If verification is expensive, speculative decoding doesn't pay off and MTP loses its inference story. If verification is cheap, you'll keep the heads around. People sometimes evaluate MTP in isolation and conclude it only gives a few points on benchmarks. The real value is systemic. You have to look at the model together with the serving stack.

Third, the training objective itself. There's a tension nobody has fully resolved. Predicting token t+2 or t+3 is a genuinely harder problem, and if you weight it too heavily you can hurt next-token quality, especially early in training. We handled it with a modest loss weight and a small number of heads, and we were fairly conservative. I think the architectures that make MTP standard will be the ones that let the model learn how far ahead to commit, rather than fixing the depth as a hyperparameter. There's a lot of room there, and it connects to the broader interest in models that plan over spans rather than one token at a time.

The counterargument I take seriously is that inference engineers already have alternatives: separate draft models, Medusa-style heads bolted on after training, Eagle, and so on. If you can retrofit speculation afterwards, why bake it into pretraining? My answer is that the retrofitted versions always lag a little in acceptance rate, because the draft and the model were never trained to agree. Co-training closes that gap. But it means the pretraining team has to care about serving, and historically those have been separate organizations. That cultural gap, more than any technical limitation, is what's slowed adoption.

So whether MTP becomes mainstream depends less on a clever new block and more on whether labs design the whole system end to end. Where that's happening, I expect it to simply become a default and stop being a talking point. Where pretraining and inference are still siloed, it'll keep looking like a nice-to-have paper trick.

r001.rationale: The response says MTP architecture should be designed end to end with the serving stack in mind, and that pretraining teams need to care about inference. It explains how inference costs and speculative decoding requirements shape architectural choices.

astra-6.text:
I think whether MTP—multi-token prediction—becomes mainstream depends on whether we design architectures that make it useful beyond an auxiliary training objective. Predicting several future tokens can provide a richer learning signal, but at inference time, those predictions also need to translate into reliable, efficient generation.

One important question is how the predictions interact. If you simply attach several independent prediction heads, you may not capture the dependencies between future tokens very well. If you make those predictions sequentially dependent, you can improve coherence, but you also introduce extra computation. The architecture has to balance those costs.

So I would look at the end-to-end result: does MTP improve model quality, and can its additional predictions reduce decoding latency enough to justify the overhead? If an architecture consistently delivers both, adopting MTP becomes a straightforward engineering choice. If the benefits are fragile or require a lot of special handling, it will remain more specialized.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing MTP’s inference benefits and costs when designing an architecture, but does not say that intended inference deployment requirements should guide the architecture chosen for pretraining.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is whether multi-token prediction becomes part of the architecture from the beginning, rather than something added afterward. Predicting several tokens is useful, but you have to consider the extra training cost, how much computation those predictions share, and whether they actually make inference faster.

For example, if the model proposes several tokens but most of them cannot be accepted, the theoretical advantage doesn’t translate into much practical value. So the architecture needs to balance the quality of those predictions with the cost of producing and verifying them.

If we can make that work with a relatively simple design, and get benefits in both training and inference, I think MTP has a strong path to becoming mainstream. But it will be the end-to-end efficiency that decides that, not just the ability to predict more tokens.

r001.rationale: The response says MTP should be built into the architecture from the beginning and discusses inference speed and efficiency. It does not clearly state that intended inference deployment requirements should guide the architecture selected for pretraining.
